processing: A green tea with tight, heavy strips and plenty of visible down; the steps specific to it are not well documented, but they follow the usual fixing, rolling and drying of Yunnan greens.
harvest_season: Spring is the usual prized picking for Yunnan green teas; no exact calendar is documented for this tea.
appearance_dry: Tight, heavy strips with showing white down.
appearance_wet: Tender, even yellowish leaf, bright in the bowl.
taste_profile: A high, lasting aroma and a fresh, rich taste with a note of honey.

brewing.notes: General advice for a sturdy Yunnan green: about 85 degrees, and cool it further if the first steep turns sharp.

vintage_note: As is usual for Chinese green teas it is sold as the current year's harvest, with early spring lots valued most, and it is best drunk within the year. It is not a tea to age.
description:
Luchun Mayu is a green tea named after Mayu, a Hani village in Qimaba township, Luchun county, in the Honghe area of southern Yunnan. Most people think of Yunnan as pu-erh and black tea, so a well-regarded green from here is worth noticing. Its nickname is the 'Long Jing of the southwest', though that is praise and not a description of the shape.

Unlike flat Long Jing, it is made in tight, heavy strips with plenty of white down. Beyond that the details of its making are thinly recorded.

The tea is known for a high, lasting aroma, a fresh and full taste, and a honeyed note, in a clear yellow-green liquor. Water around 85 degrees is a good starting point, as with other robust Yunnan greens.

Local lore says a cup used regularly for Mayu never builds up tea stains. Enjoy the story, but do not use it as a test of quality. Look instead for downy, heavy strips and ask whether the tea really comes from Luchun.
history: The tea is named for its home village, but its early history is not well recorded. Its documented reputation dates to 1980, when it was ranked among six famous teas of Yunnan at the province's first famous tea evaluation.
